reference_calls.source_slice: Marcel Ravidat,
was on a woodland stroll near Montignac with Robot,
his canine companion,
when it began sniffing at a hollow left by a toppled tree.
On 12 September 1940 he came back with three other boys for an adventurous excursion,
and the four explorers climbed down into the darkness.
In later retellings,
Ravidat embroidered his anecdote with a dramatic twist.
Robot,
he said,
had fallen into the cave.
The animal only nosed about the hole,
and the pivotal initiative was the boys' own.
Ironically,
the invented fall made the dog the hero of the story.
The artwork is usually dated to between 17,000 and 22,000 years ago;
its creators,
our distant ancestors,
lived in antiquity.
Horses,
bulls,
and stags are among the animals depicted in pigments on the murals.
Lascaux opened to the public on 14 July 1948,
and tourism brought an influx of about 1,200 visitors a day.
The throng exhaled carbon dioxide and added heat,
humidity,
and contaminants,
and the deterioration of the paintings became plain to see.
In 1963 the site closed to the public,
followed by restoration and daily inspection.
Lascaux joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1979,
and Lascaux II,
a meticulously made partial facsimile,
opened in 1983.
A white fungus invaded the walls in a 2001 outbreak,
and black stains spread after chemical treatment.
Admirers now meet the bulls only in a recreation,
the originals being inaccessible to them.
